title: NIMBioS
text:
Thousands of scientists have participated in our working groups, postdoctoral positions, tutorials, webinars, and more. We have also been a fertile ground for launching new initiatives, including the Center for the Dynamics of Social Complexity (DySoC), the Center for Analysis and Prediction of Pandemic Expansion (APPEX), and the Synergy Evaluation Institute (formerly NISER).
We maintain robust facilities for scientific computing (including our cluster Rocky, with 580 CPU and 4.5 TB RAM), and remote sensing. For more about our activities and opportunities, please peruse our menus above. Welcome!

title: Extended office hours
text:
NIMBioS offers research computing support to our community. It’s free initially; if it’s extensive work (multiple hours on an ongoing basis, such as a component of a grant) we can work up an agreement using our standard rates (but this won’t be a surprise bill – more like “this is going well, let’s start a more involved conversation”). Come talk with us! Our research programmer is Graham Derryberry, who in addition to his work at NIMBioS is an accomplished researcher in his own right. You can schedule a meeting with him for computing help, getting access to the CAS NIMBioS Rocky Cluster, and more at his scheduling page, which now features extended hours.
If you have more general questions or requests about NIMBioS, please reach out to interim director Brian O’Meara, and for queries on our spatial resources (drones! lidar! experts!) reach out to associate director Mona Papeş.

title: 2026 Rollie Lamberson Research Award – NIMBioS
text:
A paper from the Hierarchies in Conservation Working Group at the National Institute for Mathematical and Biological Synthesis just won the Rollie Lamberson Research Award: according to the award’s website, this award “is awarded to the best paper published in Natural Resource Modeling, selected for exemplifying the society’s and journal’s core mission: advancing the development and analysis of mathematical models to inform resource management and policy. Winning papers will reflect the journal’s interdisciplinary scope, drawing from fields such as forestry, fisheries, sustainability, economics, agriculture, water management, environmental science, and ecology, and contribute to the sustainable use of natural resources in the face of human and environmental pressures.”
This year, the winning paper was Armsworth, P.R., Dilkina, B., Jackson, H., Kroetz, K., Sims, C. 2025. Multilevel decision-making and protected area prioritization. Natural Resource Modeling, 38, e70004. https://doi.org/10.1111/nrm.70004. According to lead author Dr. Paul Armsworth, “The paper aims examines spatial conservation planning (where should we put protected areas to conserve species and provide benefits to people), a topic where ecologists have promoted optimization methods to help conservation organizations protect more species with their limited resources. However, these methods assume a central planner can decide where on the landscape protection will happen. In contrast, we reconcile conservation planning with the institutional constraints of our federalist system of government. Most new protected areas established in the US depend on inter-governmental grant-giving. The federal government gives grants to states and states decide where to protect, a decision shaped in part by their own priorities. In effect, we replace the scientists’ technocratic recommendation of “optimize” with a more realistic “compromise and optimize”. Through a combination of theory, algebraic example, and simulation, we show that the naïve, technocratic approach risks over-promising what land protection programs can achieve and making wasteful use of limited conservation resources. Our “compromise and optimize” approach offers much greater gains for species. The paper has its origins in a NIMBioS Working Group (Hierarchies in Conservation). The application included in the paper is for the Great Basin, chosen in part because we have other work coming forward exploring these ideas that focuses on other US geographies, including the Appalachians.”
NIMBioS is proud to have helped foster this important work. This is the second such award for NIMBioS affiliates; in 2019 a winning paper was Heins, B, Lenhart, S. and Sims, C. 2018. Assessing the economic trade-offs between prevention and suppression of forest fires. Natural Resource Modeling, 31, 31, e12159. https://doi.org/10.1111/nrm.12159

title: Welcome
text:
A strong foundation, an exciting future
As part of a significant step forward in our journey, we rebranded in 2024 and adopted a new name to reflect this new state. We are now the National Institute for Modeling Biological Systems, housed as one of the research centers and institutes within the College of Arts & Sciences at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. We’re still the NIMBioS you know and love and we are excited for this new chapter together.
We celebrate this pivotal point for NIMBioS and we express gratitude toward our founding director Dr. Lou Gross for the solid foundation NIMBioS was built upon.
Building on the strong start in life NIMBioS had as an NSF Synthesis Center, we still foster a vibrant community focused on creating new science with our models. We will continue bringing our community together as an intellectual hub for transdisciplinary research and education in the quantitative life sciences. We are focusing on our unique strength in modeling.
We are dedicated to supporting the research community and maintaining our status as an international leader, intellectual center, and emotional heart of the community of mathematical life scientists. How will we do it? We will lower the barriers for students and researchers to learn and accomplish goals within the field.
See more of our progress from 2021-4 the NIMBioS Bragbook


NIMBioS Legacy Page
We wouldn’t be where we are today without all of the great work done by previous NIMBioS staff, leaders, researchers, and students. Our Legacy website contains all archived information dating back to the start of our institute.

title: Impact
text:
NIMBioS has been an integral part of advancing the field of mathematical biology since 2008. Our programs and results have enhanced collaborations between many different academic communities, fostering convergent research and education in the United States and the world. NIMBioS has successfully survived a critical transition point in the life of the Institute. Under its initial Synthesis Center grant from NSF (2008-2021), NIMBioS received approximately $34 million dollars to establish itself as a preeminent international research institute in mathematical biology.
The impacts from this endeavor helped shape more than a decade of progress across the entire field. At the close of the initial Center grant (non-renewable after 2021), we transitioned into a new phase in which the life of NIMBioS now relies predominantly on:

providing research support and expertise in mathematical, computational, and quantitative methods, training, and outreach (either as fee-for-service through our recharge center, or as consultancies or direct subcontracts on external awards to our affiliates and staff) and, much more importantly
catalyzing additional funding proposals from affiliated researchers. Get in touch with our grant writer today!


Contribution to Public Policy and Infectious Disease Control
Contributed significantly to investigating numerous questions of direct public policy concern, particularly the analysis of the potential spread, impact and control of infectious diseases of zoonotic origin, including West Nile virus, anthrax, swine flu and mad cow disease.


Engaging Participants
Actively engaged participants to ensure that NIMBioS events welcomed and supported our whole community.


Bringing STEM to Everyone
Supported more than 280 specific education and outreach activities with more than 2,400 participants, including specific programs promoting equity in STEM.


Over 450 Projects Supported
Supported more than 450 projects proposed by the science community, leading to the publication of more than 1100 peer-reviewed scientific articles in a variety of disciplines, from anthropology to zoology.


8,700 Visits and Counting
Included more than 8,700 visits by individuals from more than 55 countries in scientific collaborative activities.


National Recognition
Received recognition for NIMBioS-supported science and research in local, regional, national and international press including Science, Nature, The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, CNN, National Public Radio, and other national media.


Reached Wider Audiences During COVID-19
Broadened reach to wider audiences via live streaming infrastructure, which has hosted more than 5,000 virtual participants in NIMBioS activities. NIMBioS Interactive, a virtual collaborative space for the NIMBioS community, was developed in response to an increased emphasis on virtual events during the 2020-2021 COVID-19 pandemic.


Online Educational Content
Produced a vast video library of more than 600 videos with more than 279,800 views and 2272 subscribers, featuring scientist interviews, science narratives, workshops, tutorials, seminars, webinars and other educational events.
